item.title: What Gardening Can Teach Us About Our Intrusive Memories
item.description:
Gratitude

What Gardening Can Teach Us About Our Intrusive Memories

Are you paying more attention to weeds than to plants?

Posted September 26, 2026

Key points
  • Unpleasant intrusive memories are annoying because they pop up randomly and trigger intense negative emotions.
  • Constantly fighting intrusive memories can feel like a game of whack-a-mole, as they often return later.
  • Your mind is like a garden. Instead of just pulling mental "weeds," actively nurture grateful memories.
  • Mentally visualizing and retrieving grateful memories helps make them more vivid and accessible over time.

Many of us have unpleasant, intrusive memories, the kind that pop into our minds randomly, like an old wound that refuses to heal. Maybe it’s a bad breakup. Or a failure at work that still haunts you. Or something hurtful a family member said to you. For me, my intrusive memories involved times when I felt humiliated or embarrassed in front of others.

What’s frustrating is their randomness. You can’t control when they enter your mind. And when they appear, they can evoke intense emotions like anger, sadness, and anxiety.

So what can you do?

Fighting Your Intrusive Memories: Weeds vs. Plants

One coping strategy to consider is to argue with your intrusive memories whenever they show up. Treat an intrusive memory like an unwanted guest. You might say, “I’m done with you. Be gone!”

If this helps you, I’m happy for you.

But for some people, fighting an intrusive memory can feel like playing whack-a-mole. The memory disappears, only to pop up again at a random moment. In this installment, I want to offer an overlooked but complementary approach to handling intrusive memories.

Recently, I spent two hours pulling weeds from my backyard. I’m not going to lie—I hate weeds. But as I was yanking out weed after weed, something occurred to me: Our minds are less of a battlefield and more of a garden.

Imagine tending your garden by spending all your time pulling weeds and doing nothing else. That’s not only exhausting; it’s counterproductive. If you’re not also nurturing your plants, they start to wither—and bare soil leaves room for weeds to return with a vengeance.

The problem with this strategy is that it’s fixated on eliminating the bad but neglects nurturing the good. So don’t just eliminate weeds. Grow your garden. Plant deliberately. Water generously. Nurture your plants.

Perhaps our memories work similarly. Don’t spend all your energy fighting intrusive memories. Nurture the positive memories that support your well-being. Give them tender loving care so that, over time, they become more vivid, accessible, and prominent in your mind.

Although there are many types of positive memories, in this article, I’ll focus on grateful memories.

Grow Your Grateful Memories

Let’s get to the nuts and bolts. How do we nurture grateful memories?

In his delightful book Memories That Matter, psychologist Jeff Singer devotes a chapter to cultivating pleasurable memories. My ideas for growing your grateful memories were inspired by this chapter.

Begin by writing down five grateful memories. Here’s how to select them.

  • Focus on memories of specific personal events. Don’t just focus on grateful thoughts. Choose memories with a story-like quality, involving a particular time, place, and sequence of events. Select a discrete event that lasted less than a day. For example, you might be grateful that your grandmother loves you, but that isn’t a specific event. Instead, you might remember your 12th birthday, when she baked your favorite matcha cheesecake and smiled broadly as she presented it to you.
  • Choose memories that evoke genuine gratitude. Select events that fill you with gratitude, not events for which you think you should feel grateful. If you don’t notice any gratitude when recalling the event, it’s probably not a good fit for this activity.
  • Choose events you can still remember reasonably vividly. Avoid stories that were told to you but that you don’t personally remember, or events for which your memory is very vague.
  • Don’t limit yourself to major life events. Seemingly ordinary moments can evoke profound gratitude.
  • Whenever possible, choose memories that reveal something important about you or your life: what you value, what brings you joy, your strengths and character, or the relationships that matter to you.

Grateful Mental Visualization

Now that you’ve identified your five grateful memories, let’s make them more vivid, emotionally rich, and retrievable.

Choose one memory, perhaps starting with the one that evokes the most gratitude. Close your eyes or soften your gaze. Imagine being transported back in time to the scene of your grateful memory. Allow yourself, as much as you can, to experience being there again.

Notice where you are. What can you see, hear, feel, or touch? Are there any tastes or smells associated with the moment? If another person is there, notice their face, expression, and voice. What do they do or say?

Don’t rush. Stay with the memory for a little while. Notice what feels especially precious about being there.

Now turn your attention to your feelings. You’ll likely feel gratitude, but notice any other emotions the memory evokes, such as joy, affection, or peace. Ask yourself: What makes this moment matter to me? What does it remind me about my life, myself, or someone I care about?

Now zoom in on one scene in the memory that feels especially meaningful. Pause there. Imagine taking a photograph of this moment. This is your grateful mental snapshot.

Notice what’s in the picture. Where are you? Who is there? What is happening? What expression is on someone’s face? Give your mental snapshot a short title that will help you retrieve it later: for example, Grandma Bringing Out the Cake, The Airport Hug, or Laughing in the Kitchen. Stay with your snapshot for a few more moments to savor it.

Practice Retrieving Your Grateful Memory

Over the next week, experiment with bringing your grateful mental snapshot to mind once a day. You don’t need to replay the entire memory. Simply bring the snapshot to mind. Notice a few of its sensory details and reconnect with the feelings or meaning it carries for you.

If an intrusive memory comes to mind, gently shift some of your attention toward your grateful snapshot and remind yourself that this experience is also part of your life. The intrusive memory may be real. But so, too, is your grateful memory.

Over the following weeks, try the same visualization exercise with your other grateful memories. Gradually, you can build a collection of vivid, meaningful memories that are easy to retrieve.

Think of your grateful memories as a small psychological library you can draw from repeatedly, rather than allowing these memories to gather dust on the shelves.

Over time, as your grateful memories begin to occupy more of your mind’s attention, you might notice a decline in how often your intrusive memories show up.

And even if you don’t have any intrusive memories, I’d still recommend the practices of grateful mental visualization and retrieving grateful memories. Because gratitude is not simply a tool for reducing our distress; it’s an outcome worth pursuing in its own right.

I’ll conclude with this passage from Singer’s book, because it beautifully captures the power of engaging with our positive memories:

“See your memory not as time frozen in the past, but as part of your present and future. The past is still alive, still seeks to be vibrant in your thoughts, and when you actively engage your memory with emotion and creativity, it does live again and grow, and so do you." (p. 159)

This article is the 4th in a mini-series on the narrative approach to understanding gratitude. It also appears in my Substack newsletter on the science and practice of gratitude.

item.title: Why Is the Department of War Against Effective Altruism?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Why Is the Department of War Against Effective Altruism?

Zero-sum thinking distorts the debate over AI safety.

Posted September 26, 2026

Key points
  • The zero-sum AI race stifles global cooperation and heightens risks.
  • Effective altruism combats biases by focusing on catastrophic risks.
  • Being overconfident in AI risk assessments isn't worse than ignoring risks altogether.
Will AI lead to human extinction?
Source: Edu Raw / Pexels

In the race for global AI dominance—economically, militarily, and so forth—some people view any attempts to slow down AI development as problematic, whether for ethical reasons, like ensuring that large language models aren’t racist, or for existential ones, like the danger of superintelligence. The premise is a winner-takes-all mentality that assumes whichever nation gets to superintelligent AI first gains global dominance.

Viewed from this mentality, one can make sense of these surreal X posts. If you see the issue as one big race between China and the United States that will determine the fate of this planet, you can make some sense of these tweets. But that’s quite a radical position to hold. Then again, politicians and the general public are prone to think of world problems as zero-sum games, where there can only be one winner and everyone else is a loser.

The Winner-Take-All Mindset

X has seen thousands of tweets over the last week about effective altruism, much of it hostile and focused on its alleged “AI doomerism.” Many effective altruists are worried that AI might have catastrophic effects, all the way from human extinction to milder ones like enabling terrorists to create bioweapons. That is true. But I’ve been puzzled by the repeated assertions by prominent people that effective altruists are an “AI doomer cult.”

I agree with many critics that it’s extremely speculative to try to evaluate the risks of AI. And different people in the AI risk debates, whether or not they are affiliated with the effective altruism movement, will have very different estimates that will appear absurd to others. We face radical uncertainty.

Personally, I do not spend much time at all thinking about the risk of human extinction due to AI, except for how AI might impact animal welfare, especially on farms. I have better things to do and leave that question to the experts. But it’s incredibly puzzling to see public intellectuals make confident assertions about the absurdity of some views when they have virtually no background in the topic. It reminds me a bit of the satirical movie, Don’t Look Up.

People who know little to nothing about AI try to smear others as idiots or cultists. If I tried to rationalize this, I think the best answer is something along the lines of: It doesn’t matter if humanity goes extinct, because it’s not worth living in a world where China wins the AI race. It’s reminiscent of the totalist view of the Nazis that asserted it didn't matter if all Germans died in a world war, since there was only one world worth living in: a world in which Germans won. And yet, I don’t think this is what we should call the most “pro-Germany" policy.

The zero-sum mindset is a cognitive bias we all share, and it is a dangerous one, for it stifles cooperation, “even in situations where cooperation is a matter of life or death.”1 If you want good political decision-making, you should make sure that actors do not suffer from a zero-sum mindset.

Risk Assessment and Human Psychology

Another distinguishing feature of effective altruists, in their attempts to counter cognitive biases, is a deliberate emphasis on countering our human psychology, which tends to disregard tiny risks or treat them as almost certain. In general, humans are pretty awful at probabilistic reasoning.2 So it’s good to try and study these risks in whatever way we can to turn uncertainty into manageable risk.

Another criticism of effective altruists is that they’ve gone all-in on “crazy” longtermism, thinking only about the long-term future and AI risk while neglecting the present. That’s far from the truth.

Luke Moore, Senior Partnerships Manager at Giving What We Can, broke down the effective altruism funding environment in a post on the Effective Altruism Forum for 2026:

~50% to global health

~30% to global catastrophic risk reduction (up from ~20% in 2024)

~10% to animal welfare

~5% to climate change mitigation

(The rest is unknown or a bit harder to categorise: ~5%)

Longtermism as a Necessary Counterweight

I, for one, think it’s great that someone is concerned with global catastrophic risks. If it wasn’t for effective altruists, there would be very little funding available to actually do serious research in this area. But my attitude is really a risk-balancing one here. You might think that longtermism—roughly, the view that we should not discriminate against future humans (or animals) just because they will live in the future—is a crazy philosophical view. If there are billions of humans who could live in the future and we ought to take them into account, our political decisions might look radically different. But humans, as a species, and our institutions along with them, are so ridiculously short-termist that it hardly matters if longtermism as a philosophy is mistaken or ridiculous. They offer a good counterweight.

However, in the AI space, you might think that this is not true. Perhaps, as critics lament, longtermists/effective altruists (the latter does not imply the former) dominate this discourse. I am skeptical. Effective altruists share visible platforms and counterarguments, and are prominent in the space. But let’s grant they are actually overrepresented.

Still, effective altruists are generally not AI doomers. They are just trying to estimate what the actual risks are. Likely, many are overconfident in their own assessments. (So is everyone.) Some will no doubt appear like the “crazy” performance Leonardo DiCaprio gave in Don’t Look Up, when others sought to downplay these risks entirely. But so what?

Individual Assessment vs. Collective Ignorance

I think some of the estimates given by researchers are blatantly outrageous in their confidence. But so what? None of that is a reason to ignore low-probability risks. People confuse individual assessments with communities of epistemic peers trying to get at the truth.

Overconfidence in these estimates by individuals is not worse (however ludicrous they may be) than collective ignorance towards unknown risks altogether.

item.title: Rethinking Self-Control in the Age of GLP-1s
item.description:
Self-Control

Rethinking Self-Control in the Age of GLP-1s

Why GLP-1s are setting a new direction for behavior change support.

Posted September 26, 2026

Key points
  • Being overweight or obese is often seen as a failure of personal willpower.
  • Traditional diets fail at long-term maintenance, with most people regaining lost weight within five years.
  • GLP-1s disrupt our idea of willpower by quieting "food noise" and helping break automatic eating habits.
  • GLP-1s may offer a window to build lasting habits with behavioural support.

Who is to blame for excess body weight?

It is a deeply loaded question, and one to which many people silently hold a firm answer: Excess weight is fundamentally an individual failure of self-control. On social media, in policy debates, and across everyday conversations, one cultural narrative has seemingly persisted—that some people simply have the discipline to resist temptation, while others just do not.

In behavioural science, self-control is formally defined as an individual’s ability to modify or override their internal thoughts, emotions, and impulsive actions in order to align with their long-term goals. Academics conceptualise this in distinct ways. Some view it through the lens of "ego depletion"—self-control as a finite personal reserve, like a muscle, that fatigues with overuse—while others see it as a self-correcting feedback loop, or as a dynamic interaction between our reflective mind and our impulsive, automatic drives.

A competing narrative argues that, in a world where almost half of the global population is living with overweight or obesity, body weight is not a personal failure at all, but rather a context failure. In this view, we are all swamped by a toxic, hyper-palatable food environment that has been explicitly engineered to overwhelm our conscious restraint.

The Limits of Self-Control

Distinguishing between these narratives is important as it dictates where we focus our energy when it comes to prevention.

If weight is primarily a contextual problem, the solution then lies in reorganizing the food system. Environmental nudges, like reducing portion sizes or reformulating products offer broad-spectrum fixes that can support the majority of the population. The trade-off? Critics argue this approach is paternalistic and penalizes consumer freedom.

Conversely, if weight is viewed as a self-control failure, the solution is advice and skill-building targeted at the individual. This line of thinking has sparked an abundance of digital health apps and counselling services designed to boost personal self-control resources - all widely available while population-level obesity continues to rise unabated.

Indeed, one of the more fundamental issues when it comes to existing self-control-based approaches is not in successfully initiating weight loss, but in maintaining it over time. Decades of research show that while dietary behaviour change interventions can lead to significant short-term weight loss, between one-to-two thirds of weight is usually regained in a year, and nearly all is back on within five.

The GLP-1 Disruption: Biology vs. Environment

Enter GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1s). These medications are attracting global attention for helping users to achieve weight losses of up to 20 percent when adherence is optimal—a shift that is challenging some of our core assumptions about dietary self-control.

Firstly, GLP-1s are demonstrating that weight management is not merely a self-regulation failure. By modulating central reward pathways and gut-brain signalling, these drugs clearly reveal that "willpower" can be pharmacologically altered.

Secondly, GLP-1s are also highlighting that we are not helpless victims of our environment either. By quieting intrusive "food noise," these medications allow users to break out of the automatic trigger-response-reward habit loop when it comes to their diet, proving that environmental cues can in fact be successfully managed.

New Solution, Same Problem

Despite impressive early results, emerging longer-term data is starting to reveal a familiar pattern when it comes to maintenance, however: significant weight re-gain when medications are eventually stopped.

Notably, in the GLP-1 era, this rebound carries unique risks because pharmacologically induced weight loss can be exceptionally deep and rapid. As a result, it is often accompanied by muscle loss, which subsequently alters metabolic rate and exacerbates outcomes such as sarcopenic obesity.

From a more psychological lens, another critical issue for GLP-1 users lies in causal attribution. When weight loss is primarily driven by a weekly injection, individuals are naturally inclined to attribute successes to an external agent, rather than developing an internal locus of control and building their dietary self-efficacy.

This is a risky attribution over the long term. Relying on lifelong pharmacological appetite suppression, with all its associated financial costs, gastrointestinal side effects, and potential nutritional deficiencies, is neither a realistic nor complete solution for everyone.

Skill-Building in the Quiet Space

Yet GLP-1s do not have to automatically render dietary self-control obsolete.

Instead, they may in fact be opening up a powerful new window of opportunity to train self-regulation skills through dedicated lifestyle behaviour change programs tailored to the unique obstacles faced by users throughout their weight loss journey.

For example, we might start by capitalizing on the new period of quiet at the beginning of treatment. The moment so-called food noise starts to wane presents a golden opening when individuals may finally have the cognitive bandwidth to absorb self-regulation skills, learn how to manage environmental triggers, and build positive habit loops without fighting a constant impulse control war.

As treatment progresses, programs must sustain engagement through side effects. This means offering practical strategies to manage outcomes like nausea before they cause premature drop-off. It also means helping patients navigate a blunted dopaminergic reward system. As medication reduces pleasure derived from food or alcohol, effective behaviour change support should guide individuals toward cultivating alternative, non-nutritional sources of reward to ensure change are not just made, but maintained.

Finally, and perhaps most importantly, we must plan for the transition off the medication and relapse prevention. Here, interventions should actively help users internalize their achievements, re-attributing progress to their daily choices rather ascribing it solely to the drug.

The New Era of Behavioural Weight Management

A recent study exploring perceptions of those losing weight with GLP-1s versus behaviour change or bariatric surgery presents an eye-opening finding: individuals who lost weight using medication were rated as less competent, less popular, and even less moral by onlookers, while also being assumed to have poorer lifestyle habits even without any information to base this viewpoint on.

These results show that even as the conversation evolves in this new era of weight management, social assumptions around the moral value of willpower remain close to the surface. Yet GLP-1s continue to demonstrate that self-control can clearly benefit from a biological boost. By dampening hunger and quieting food noise, these medications are helping more and more people break deeply entrenched behavioural patterns, offering a vital window of opportunity for healthier habits to take root, provided they are paired with dedicated support services designed for that exact purpose.

item.title: Why Do We Fall in Love With People Who Are Bad for Us?
item.description:
Mating

Why Do We Fall in Love With People Who Are Bad for Us?

Romantic attraction and partner suitability often point in opposite directions.

Posted September 26, 2026

Key points
  • "Checklists" in dating rarely rank qualities by importance and often ignore the crucial issue of suitability.
  • Choosing a suitable romantic partner requires more than counting strengths and weaknesses.
  • The ability of partners to bring out the best in one another is a hallmark of flourishing relationships.
Source: Skylake/Pexels

"All good things are difficult to achieve; and bad things are very easy to get."—Confucius

Choosing a romantic partner is complex. We may focus on a person's strengths and weaknesses, but simply counting them does not show whether that person is right for us. A most common mistake in romantic choice is assuming that attraction and suitability are the same thing. They often overlap, but sometimes they point in opposite directions.

The Paradox of Falling in Love With the Wrong Person

"I knew from the beginning that he was bad for me, but the sex was great."—A divorcee

"I loved my former spouse dearly, but his insistence on an open marriage was bad for me."—A divorcee

From an evolutionary perspective, detecting negative events is more important than detecting positive ones. Negative events may threaten our survival, whereas positive ones merely offer opportunities to improve our situation. Accordingly, bad experiences, negative emotions, and critical feedback usually have a greater psychological impact than positive ones. We are more motivated to avoid bad outcomes than to pursue good ones (Baumeister et al., 2001).

This negativity bias is most relevant to romantic relationships. Negative qualities can undermine a relationship and seriously harm a partner. By contrast, people often adapt to the absence of certain positive qualities. John Gottman argued that lasting relationships require substantially more positive than negative interactions.

3 Reasons We Fall in Love With the Wrong Person

Given the weight we assign to negative qualities, why do we sometimes fall in love with people who are clearly bad for us? I suggest three reasons.

1. The Attractiveness and Personality Halos

“Our love is a flame, burning within.”—Suzi Quarto

"We sapiosexuals are sexually attracted to highly intelligent people, regardless of looks."—Marlène Schiappa

Falling in love involves two major dimensions: attractiveness and praiseworthiness. Attractiveness draws us toward someone; praiseworthiness reflects our broader evaluation of that person's character and accomplishments.

These dimensions often influence each other. In the attractiveness halo effect, physically attractive people are perceived as more intelligent, sociable, and morally admirable than they actually are (Batres & Shiramizu, 2023). The reverse also occurs. Intelligence, kindness, humor, and wisdom can increase a person's attractiveness, a phenomenon sometimes called the personality halo. In this sense, intelligence itself can become a source of sexual attraction, as in sapiosexuality. As a result, the person who attracts us most intensely is not always the one best suited for a long-term relationship. Strong attraction can obscure deeper incompatibilities, making an unsuitable relationship harder to recognize and harder to leave.

2. The Checklist Trap

"There is no perfection, only beautiful versions of brokenness."—Shannon L. Alder

A popular approach to partner selection is to create a checklist of desired qualities. This approach has two significant weaknesses. First, checklists rarely establish a hierarchy of importance. Thus, height, kindness, intelligence, and humor may appear as separate boxes to tick even though they differ greatly in significance. This reduces a complex person to a collection of disconnected traits. Second, checklists often overlook the issue of suitability: someone may possess many qualities we desire and still be the wrong partner for us.

The central issue is not the number of desirable qualities a person possesses, but which qualities matter most and how well they fit with our own characteristics, values, and aspirations. Romantic suitability is a matter of identifying the qualities that are most important and understanding how they function within our relationship (Ben-Ze'ev, 2019).

3. Counting Superficial Flaws Instead of Assessing Incompatibility

"The art of being wise is the art of knowing what to overlook."—William James

A more sophisticated strategy is to focus on major flaws rather than cataloguing every minor imperfection. Since everyone has shortcomings, many minor flaws can be accommodated within a healthy relationship. Major flaws, however, may threaten its very foundation. The problem is that profound flaws are often harder to detect than superficial ones. Physical appearance can be assessed quickly, whereas selfishness, emotional unavailability, unreliability, or deep incompatibility often emerge only over time. A one-night stand may reveal a great deal about attraction while telling little about the capacity for a flourishing, enduring relationship.

Detecting incompatibility is more difficult than counting flaws. What matters is not the number of shortcomings, but their nature and their consequences for the relationship.

The Importance of Bringing Out the Best in Each Other

"You make me want to be a better man."—As Good as It Gets

Identifying negative qualities is important, but some positive qualities may matter even more. Among the most important is the partners' ability to bring out the best in one another. Research on the Michelangelo phenomenon suggests that close partners can help us move toward our ideal selves. When a partner treats us in ways that support our aspirations, we become closer to who we want to become. Just as Michelangelo was said to reveal the figure hidden within the marble, romantic partners can help "sculpt" one another toward their better selves (Drigotas, 2002).

This quality is difficult to identify early in a relationship because it emerges through shared experiences over time. It cannot be captured by a checklist; rather, recognizing it often requires the kind of intuition experts use when information is incomplete. Indeed, effective rules of thumb focus on the most important information while ignoring much of the rest (Gigerenzer, 2007). In romantic choice, this means paying less attention to the total number of desirable qualities and more attention to a few deep ones.

Concluding Thoughts

"Only those who know when enough is enough will ever have enough."—Lao Tzu

Finding a suitable romantic partner requires more than counting strengths and weaknesses. Focusing on the number of flaws may cause us to overlook deeper incompatibilities. Some of the most important relationship qualities emerge only through time and shared experience. Our goal is not to find someone without flaws or someone who possesses the greatest number of desirable traits; it is rather to identify the qualities that matter most for mutual flourishing. Romantic attraction answers the question, "Who do I want?" Romantic suitability answers the deeper question, "With whom can I flourish?" The two often overlap, but not always. Sometimes, the person who attracts us most strongly is not the person who is best for us. The challenge is telling the difference.

item.title: Why Chronic Pain Causes Emotional Pain
item.description:
Chronic Pain

Why Chronic Pain Causes Emotional Pain

Chronic pain extends beyond the physical body and affects the emotions.

Posted September 26, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows a link between chronic pain and issues like anxiety, anger, and depression.
  • Many common emotional problems are bidirectionally related to chronic pain.
  • Functional limitations caused by chronic pain can result in emotional distress.

We tend to view chronic pain (CP) as a body issue; a problem that lives mainly within our physical system and causes tangible aches, pain, stiffness, tightness, soreness, and general discomfort. But there is an emotional component to chronic pain that is often either overlooked or misunderstood. Understanding the intersection of physical pain and emotional pain is necessary in taking a holistic view of the body-mind dyad.

The Research

This correlation between physical pain and emotional distress continues to be of great interest, and recent research indicates that around 40 percent of individuals with chronic pain experience clinically significant symptoms of depression or anxiety and that “the co-occurrence of chronic pain with depression and anxiety is a significant public health concern” (Aaron et al., 2025).

Meta-analyzed data from 110 studies revealed that among individuals who experienced CP, a range of psychological problems were observed, including depression, anxiety, somatization, anger, low self-esteem, and disturbance to normal emotional functioning (Burke et al., 2015).

A 2025 umbrella review concluded that CP and mental disorders frequently co-occur and reported evidence of bidirectional relationships, particularly between depression and chronic pain (Stubbs et al., 2025). This undeniable relationship between the physical and the emotional can help us better understand why and how CP can directly affect emotional functioning.

Depression: “My Body Is Betraying Me”

Clinically speaking, depression is often associated with feelings of hopelessness and helplessness, and for individuals with CP, this sense of helplessness is driven by the feeling that their physical body is failing or betraying them.

CP might be considered a “stress state,” wherein a person is in a constant state of discomfort. After a prolonged period, a stress state inevitably leads to exhaustion, fatigue, and hypoactivity (low mood).

CP is defined as a recurrent or persistent pain that lasts longer than three months (Raffaeli et al., 2021). For some people, CP lasts far longer than three months and can persist for decades. Existing in this constant stress state has significant neurobiological consequences that invite depression, including changes in brain chemistry, overactivation of the brain’s stress-response system, and the shrinking of key brain areas (Tafet & Nemeroff, 2015).

The prolonged fatigue and negative feelings of body betrayal that come with CP can result in depression and lead to maladaptive responses such as social withdrawal, inability to access adaptive coping mechanisms, and continued low mood (Boyes, 2013).

Anxiety: “What if I Never Get Better?”

CP and anxiety share a complex, bidirectional relationship: Persistent physical pain causes fear and stress and, at the same time, constant anxiety and fear can cause inflammation, resulting in a vicious cycle (McAllister, 2010).

The fear associated with CP often takes the form of catastrophic thinking, such as “What if this gets worse? What if I never feel better? What if this indicates a much larger problem?” Studies find that among people with CP, anxiety responses such as rumination, fixation, avoidance, and cognitive fusion (interpreting thoughts as literal facts) are common (Tenti et al., 2026). The “what ifs” of CP-related anxiety can cause distress: Rumination and fixation cause us to struggle to pay attention to anything other than our physical pain; avoidance can cause us to neglect care and pain management; and cognitive fusion can cause us to misinterpret our thoughts and overestimate negative outcomes.

Anger: “I Hate Feeling This Way”

Similar to anxiety, anger is bidirectionally related to CP: Pain can trigger frustration while frustration and anger can worsen inflammation. As with depression and anxiety, anger is commonly observed as having a close relationship with CP.

According to the Mayo Clinic, many people with CP “report feeling angry at themselves or at others on a consistent basis” (Mayo Clinic, 2024). A staggering 70 percent of people with CP report feeling angry at themselves or at their healthcare providers (Black, 2020). Furthermore, some individuals with CP feel a sense of injustice or unfairness, a sense of “why me?” regarding their pain.

While expressions of anger can be coping mechanisms for living with pain, pain management doctor Germaine Rowe points out that it can be counterproductive, as it “puts the body in a state of stress,” causing “a chain of events that end up worsening the pain” (Black, 2020).

Emotional Dysfunction: “I Don’t Feel Like Myself”

To bring it all together and appropriately understand this important connection between CP and emotional functioning, we must accept that CP often causes individuals to feel detached from themselves or from the way they are accustomed to functioning. These functional limitations directly cause emotional dysfunction in the form of depression, anxiety, and anger.

Accepting the viewpoint that there is an undeniable relationship between the physical and the emotional can help us better understand why and how CP affects an individual’s emotional life and recognize that these two parts of our existence are not mutually exclusive.

item.title: How Teens Can Effectively Respond to Their Insecurity
item.description:
Adolescence

How Teens Can Effectively Respond to Their Insecurity

Carving out a unique life path helps teens navigate past anxiety.

Posted September 26, 2026

Key points
  • Insecurity as a normal adolescent experience and challenge.
  • Many teenagers act like sheep, seeking peer attention and approval in their quest to feel secure.
  • Young people who earn lifetime success act like GOATs, following their unique path up to the mountaintop.

Insecure.

That’s the best word to characterize the adolescent years, including young athletes, based on my 50-plus years of experience working with youth. (Please don’t do the age math on that.) Poetically phrased, insecurity is the essence of adolescence.

A few of the general sources of anxiety young people have shared with me over the years include the experience of getting older, the ensuing loss of childhood, and the terror of approaching adulthood.

Kids entering middle school express being intimidated by the older kids in the building, perceiving them as being in their late teens or early 20s. Trying to figure out how to be a teenager and their bodily changes are other shared challenges.

High school freshmen and sophomores are burdened with feeling immature and undersized. They also struggle with trying to figure out how to appear older and more mature. Juniors and seniors are saddled with the college application process and the realization that high school will soon be ending and that they’ll be leaving home for their post-secondary education.

Adding to all that anxiety-fueled insecurity for teen athletes is the worry about tryouts, playing time, and the future of their sports career hanging in the air.

College is next, as they enter a new world minus family and friends at their side. It’s off to strangers in a strange land. Ninety-four percent of high school athletes face the end of their sports careers as they enter college.

Entering the adult world, post-college has its own daunting, terrifying challenges, as we can all relate to from our own experience,

Insecurity about all that stuff is perfectly normal and goes hand-in-hand with the human growth process. It’s how young people respond to the thoughts and feelings accompanying their insecurity that will ultimately determine effective or ineffective living.

A Common Adolescent Response to Insecurity

Many adolescents act like this guy, following a herd of peers to cope with their insecurity.
Source: Dick Pothen/Pexels

Kids do what they believe will impress, grab attention, and get them aligned with the cool kids. Instead, they become scripted by other people and fail to discover and follow their own unique life path.

John Waldron, the president of Goldman-Sachs, described such behavior as “the peacock phenomenon” during an interview I conducted with him a few years ago. He agreed that all people doing that (not just the young) are insecure.

Thirsting to rid themselves of unpleasant thoughts and feelings of insecurity, many young people seek to feel better by following and clinging to peers. They thoughtlessly and carelessly do anything to gain inclusion to allay yucky feelings. It’s what acceptance and commitment training (ACT) calls experiential avoidance—doing things just to avoid intense, displeasing emotion.

Here are examples of such adolescent behavior:

  • Kids vaping, drinking, or smoking marijuana just to fit in with a peer group.
  • Teen athletes bullying teammates and others—what teens call “rage-baiting”— just to get a laugh and gain the approval and acceptance of the cool, arrogant member of the team; then drinking up a storm at team parties for the same purpose.
  • College kids who do anything in the sorority or fraternity “rush” process. They gain relief by the acquisition of “sisters” and “brothers” as security blankets, engaging in endless partying and other typical frat and sorority craziness.

These kinds of middle school, high school, and college kids act like sheep, following the herd. They end up doing things that deliver short-term relief from anxiety. They go down a path that isn’t their own and can lead to self-destruction, like getting high, drinking, and other harmful activities.

How Successful People Responded

GOATs follow their own path to the top of mountains.
Source: Image created by Google Gemini AI.

Those who turned out to be successful weren’t sheep. They sought to be the GOAT (Greatest of All Time). They were a bit insecure in their youth, according to them, but rarely compromised themselves in the need for security. They were too busy following their own path in pursuit of what was important to them.

Examples of successful people I observed and was blessed to know as they were growing up include John Waldron, Tom Modly, the former Secretary of the United States Navy, John Bell, the frontman for the iconic rock band Widespread Panic, and a plethora of others. They weren’t attention-seekers.

At the time, I ascribed their quiet demeanor to shyness. I was completely wrong. They were too busy following their own path and doing what was truly meaningful to them. They weren’t obsessed with trying to fit in with peers and couldn’t have cared less about that.

Moral of the Story

“Do not go where the path may lead, go where there is no path and leave a trail,” American philosopher Ralph Waldo Emerson advised. Stop seeking security by aimlessly following others and create your own life trail. Set your sights on what you want to achieve and set goals detailing the action steps you’ll take to climb to the mountaintop you seek.

Instead of being a sheep, try being a GOAT. Sheep just follow the herd, losing their individuality with a herd mentality. GOATs climb mountains, blazing their own unique trail en route to the top.

Give it a shot, young people, be it in athletics or anything else you strive for.
